text: Lesson 4's Dev-stage diagram included a step called Branch Created, and Lesson 6's CI/CD pipeline starts the instant a developer pushes a change to Git — both assumed you already knew roughly what that meant. This lesson opens that up.

A repository is the full tracked history of a project — every file, plus every change ever made, back to the first commit. A commit is a saved snapshot of changes, with a message describing what changed and why. A branch is an isolated line of work, split off so changes in progress don't affect anyone else until merged back — that's exactly the Branch Created step from Lesson 4's diagram. And a remote is a hosted copy of the repository, most commonly on GitHub, so a whole team shares the same history.

A typical change, start to finish: clone the repo to your own machine, create and switch to a new branch, make your changes, stage them, commit with a message, and push the branch to the remote. From there you open a pull request — a teammate reads the diff and approves it, exactly the Code Review step from Lesson 4 — before it ever merges into the shared history.

A commit message like fixed stuff is technically a message, but it's useless to the next person reading the history — including you, six months from now. And a dot-gitignore file tells Git which files to never track in the first place: build output, local configuration, and especially credentials, since a committed password stays recoverable from history forever, even after you delete the file in a later commit.
Next lesson: releases, deployments, and CI/CD — the machinery that actually moves a Git commit into a live, running system.
